target_customer: Underserved communities and local governments in India that use and fund shared toilet facilities; funded mainly by donors and grants
problem: Open defecation remains common in India and household toilets are often unavailable or unused; shared toilets need reliable maintenance and funding.
business_model: Nonprofit running shared toilet facilities, with biogas powered water purification sold locally to cover costs, supported by grants and donations

founders.name: Anoop Jain
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (March 2016) says he studied environmental engineering at Northwestern and designed the biogas to water purification system; a doctoral student per a WGBH headline.

technical_complexity.rationale: Biodigesters, water purification and field operations in Bihar combine standard engineering with hard operating conditions.

defensibility.rationale: As a nonprofit its advantage is operating experience and community trust; larger groups like Sulabh and government programs could replicate the model.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: TechCrunch noted the government's large sanitation commitment as a potential funder; the organization stayed independent and by 2026 reports 27 facilities.

market_need_then: The 2026 site says nearly 100 million Indians lack toilet access; in 2016 TechCrunch cited a government commitment of $30 billion to end open defecation.

branding.name_origin: Acronym of Sanitation and Health Rights in India; Fast Company and The Better India say it was formerly known as Humanure (Power)
branding.brand_signature: Poop to methane to clean water story

rebrands.to: Sanitation and Health Rights in India (SHRI)
rebrands.why: Not stated in sources; date unknown

branding.community_and_virality: Wide coverage in TechCrunch, Fast Company, WGBH, The Better India and Global Citizen; awards including the 2014 Waislitz Global Citizen Award winner listing.

brand_strength.rationale: A vivid toilet to water story drove press and awards, but evidence of brand-driven donations or growth is limited.

pivots.from: Original plan for nutrition work in Bihar
pivots.why: TechCrunch says Jain shifted after learning open defecation was the larger health problem; later the model moved toward renovating and managing shared toilets (company site)

outcome_analysis: SHRI is a nonprofit that survived and kept operating, reporting 27 facilities and 2.51 million uses on its 2026 site. It relied on small grants, donors and YC exposure rather than venture rounds, so its story is steady mission driven operation rather than a financial outcome.
notes: Nonprofit, so rounds are grants not equity; a 2018 GlobalGiving report mentions multi-year funding agreements (for example two facilities in Assam) without amounts. Founding year conflicts (2010 per Boston University, 2011 per India Sanitation Coalition, 2012 first grant), so founded_year is null. Competitors: TechCrunch names none, and the only found sources on Sulabh International are dated 2007 or later than the batch, so the list is empty. No closure news found. The YC listing says team size 1.
